## Summary
Lenses checked: correctness, silent-failure, tests, comments.
`m0003_drop_legacy_email` must be fixed before merge: it drops `users.legacy_email` without taking a backup first, so the data is lost for good. The other destructive migrations in this repository back up the table before they drop anything.

## Changes
This pull request adds migration `m0003`, which drops `users.legacy_email`, and migration `m0004`, which backs up `orders` and then drops `orders.coupon_code`. It also adds one test that runs migrations 1 to 4 in order and checks that both columns are gone and that `orders_backup_4` was created.

## Critical
- migrations/m0003_drop_legacy_email.py:7 — correctness — Call backup_table before dropping users.legacy_email — On any database with existing `users` rows, `upgrade` runs `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_email` without calling `backup_table`, so no `users_backup_3` exists. `migrations/safety.py:3-5` says "each destructive migration first calls backup_table", and both `m0002` and `m0004` do. — Rolling back the deploy cannot bring back `legacy_email` values, and `restore_table(conn, "users", 3)` fails because the backup table does not exist. — Fix: Add `backup_table(conn, "users", VERSION)` before the drop, as `migrations/m0002_drop_nickname.py:7` does, and extend `test_drop_retired_columns` to insert a `users` row and assert that `users_backup_3` holds it.
